newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 18.

text.p: The National Party is considering delaying or ultimately scrapping its second round of tax cuts to accommodate NZ First's demands for increased spending and a compulsory superannuation scheme. The move would be a big backdown for National but could give it the inside running on a coalition with NZ First. Labour remains strongly resistant to a compulsory superannuation scheme. National Party sources said on Sunday that "phasing" of the second round of tax cuts, which has already been passed into law and is due to take effect on July 1, 1997, was now under consideration. No final decision had been made. Page 1.

Compulsory superannuation -- a key NZ First policy plank -- was denounced by the Council of Trade Unions on Sunday. Council secretary Angela Foulkes, who sat on the Todd taskforce that reviewed superannuation policy, said docking people's pay and putting the money aside for their retirement was inequitable, inefficient and unworkable. Page 2.

Thousands of New Zealanders were driving death-trap cars because of a scandal "of Cave Creek proportions", Labour MP Harry Duynhoven alleged on Sunday. Many people had probably died or been seriously injured as a result of the Land Transport Safety Authority's failure to protect the public, he said. Duynhoven claimed the authority had suppressed its findings that some models of cars were "horribly unsafe". Page 3.

With inflation pressures from food prices and a possible resurgence in the housing market the Reserve Bank could be forced to keep a tight hold on monetary policy despite softening labour conditions, according to the ANZ Bank. A "modest easing" may be possible in the first half of next year. Page 13.

Dublin's Independent Newspapers has 85 percent of Wilson and Horton after extending its $11-a-share takeover offer for the company by a week last Friday. Wilson and Horton shares finished at $11.06 after 63,075 shares were traded. INP managing director of international operations Brendan Hopkins said the company was
happy with the level it had achieved. There would be no further stands in the market. Page 13.

Radio Network's acquisition of Prospect Radio from Britain's GWR Group was further evidence of the company's commitment to the New Zealand radio industry, chief executive Joan Withers said. Prospect, which has 12 radio stations in Auckland and Hamilton, was bought by Radio Network for $40 million. The Radio Network -- formerly the government-owned Radio NZ Commercial -- is owned by a consortium of domestic and international media and communications operations. Page 13.

NZ First's coalition talks are turning the corner into the home straight and its preferred partner may be reasonably clear by the end of this week, according to a source in the talks. But with party caucuses to be briefed on Tuesday and consulted over the hard bargaining that is expected to dominate this week's negotiations, the preference is unlikely to be declared for at least another week after that.

Transport officials have been accused of suppressing studies that show many New Zealand cars are unsafe. Some of the most popular makes and models on our roads have been labelled "death traps", by the author of a used car buying guide being released on Monday.

The deputy leader of NZ First, Tau Henare, has accused Reserve Bank governor Don Brash of "unsolicited interference" in the political process. In a newspaper column on Sunday, Henare said in was not Brash's job to comment on government spending decisions.

The company which runs Newstalk ZB and Classic Hits 97FM has taken control of a clutch of other Auckland radio stations including The Breeze and Hauraki. Under a $40 million deal hammered out during complex negotiations, The Radio Network of New Zealand -- which in April bought Radio New Zealand's 41 commercial stations -- has bought a further 12 stations from the British company GWR Group Plc. But under the terms of Commerce Commission approval, a number of frequencies will have to be sold.

Senior government officials from Latin America and Asia will fly into New Zealand early next month to study how former state-run enterprises have been corporatised and privatised. The conference, to be held in Wellington from December 8-12, is being run under the auspices of the World Bank. The Zealand organiser is Ernst and Young.

Commercial property investment had enthusiastic reviews this year. Rental increases are predicted to be in the offing because of a rising shortage of quality leasable space. In the investment years to July and August, commercial property paid
higher gross returns to local investors than cash, fixed interest and shares.
